utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is the last day of final argument. I would first like to give the floor to the Prosecution for their one and a half hours of remaining time to address the Court. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, throughout the course of our closing submissions, we have explained with many examples the Defence's reliance in its final brief on mischaracterised, unreliable, out-of-context or even non-existent evidence in support of inaccurate representations about the case. Their closing submissions saw no departure from that approach, which was instead augmented by faulty lessons in evidence analysis, transparent attempts to misuse procedural safe-guards like the burden of proof as weapons of attack, and flailing attacks against the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber, and indeed the world, the accuracy of which was inversely proportional to the stridency. Ignoring four and a half years of trial and a voluminous evidential record replete with one damning document or contemporaneous witness observation after another, they claim that General Mladic is on trial simply because he is a Serb and attempt to justify this baseless accusation in a variety of ways. They accuse the Prosecution of turning the burden of proof "upside down." Why? Because the Prosecution in the first of its submissions "was talking about a lot of things that they said we didn't prove in our final brief." And the Defence claims: "We don't have to prove the things in our final brief." But no one said that they have to prove or even say anything. Unfortunately for them, however, once they choose to do so, it is permissible, even obligatory, to explore the evidence that supposedly supports it. And as we demonstrated over and again in our final brief and again during submissions, the Defence relies on evidence that does not support what they claim or that has been mischaracterised or that comes from unreliable witnesses or that otherwise upon closer examination does not support the proposition. Having falsely claimed that their misrepresentations -- or, excuse me, falsely claimed that exposing their misrepresentations is improper, they Defence doubles down by claiming that the very act of doing so creates reasonable doubt. "Why are they talking about our case instead of theirs? That means that they've lost." For the Defence, the more times their arguments are exposed as false, even misleading, the weaker the Prosecution case becomes. The absurdity of that proposition is made even more clear by the fact that demonstration of the false Defence propositions invariably led, as we repeatedly underscored, to the confirmation of the Prosecution's case and the proof of the allegations in the indictment. For example, the Defence accuses the Prosecution of a clear effort, they say, to manipulate court staff by referring to Karadzic in a case against Mladic. It's an attempt, they say, at guilt by association, playing on emotions. This is again a transparent attempt to deflect from damning evidence. References to Karadzic, Mladic's only superior in the chain of command and key partner in implementing all four JCEs, began with a debunking of Mladic's attempt to place the exclusive blame for the illegal Directive 7 on Karadzic. And those references moved on to the many ways in which Karadzic's statements and conduct so clearly illuminate Mladic's guilt, including the fact that it was Karadzic, already committed to and implementing the ethnic cleansing campaign in Bosnia, who asked for Mladic in order to implement his objectives on the basis of Mladic's efforts in Croatia; that even before General Mladic formally assumed the position of chief of the Main Staff he worked with Karadzic to come up with the strategic objectives, that is, ethnic separation and where they would create it; that Karadzic and Mladic agreed that this was an historical opportunity to create a state with few internal enemies; agreed that achieving the factual situation was crucial; agreed that "all means" or "reciprocal" means were justified in the face of a genocidal struggle; and worked in tandem throughout the war to achieve the goals as the men who were, in the words of the Foca Crisis Staff president, "our leaders." And yet the Defence claims or pretends that mentioning Karadzic is an act of manipulation. Another straw man argument was the repeated claim that the Prosecution on the first day asked you to accept what it considers the "better" conclusion or "better" version, which to the Defence ipso facto raises reasonable doubt. Now, as an initial matter, the word "better" was used only three times that day: Once to quote General Mladic using that word at the time; once to quote an SDS newspaper about the genetically murderous Croat desire to kill the "better" Serbs, and once to quote an SRK assistant commander's message to the troops that Serbs were genetically superior to Muslims - "stronger, better, more handsome and cleverer." The single alleged example the Defence cited was the Prosecution challenge to the Defence claim that the word "liberate" meant only "fighting against aggression," when we noted that a more accurate understanding of the word, belying the Defence claim of a benign and exclusive meaning, could be found in its use in a meeting of locals with Mladic and Karadzic, where it was reported that: "There are no Muslims now in Bratunac municipality. It is a fully liberated town." We did not suggest that while the Defence position was reasonable there was another possibility. We addressed the supposed alternative views offered by the Defence and explained that it was not reasonable and that when closely examined, in fact, proved the Prosecution case. Again, that claim is a transparent effort by the Defence to deflect attention from exposure of the misrepresentations upon which they relied and the evidence which demonstrates Mladic's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The Defence made clear what they need you to do in order to avoid the otherwise inevitable conclusion. They need to you look at the evidence unreasonably, by isolating only the evidence they want you to consider or by accepting fanciful interpretations of evidence. They made that apparent with the first example. The video reflecting General Mladic entering Srebrenica and saying the time has come to take revenge on the Turks, tossing out increasingly imaginative interpretations, including that a glowering Mladic was suggesting killing Muslims with kindness, that is, "taking the moral high ground" and thus making the enemy forces irate. Seriously, that was the argument. This is not only unreasonable on its face, particularly given the reference to bitter history - the rebellion of the Dahis - but completely ignores the weight of the evidence which must inform any attempt to interpret this video and thus give it proper weight and understanding. Other examples of the effort to spin meaningless or even invented arguments into threads of reasonable doubt include: The claim that the RS did not declare a legal state of war, essentially an irrelevancy. First, many RS laws invoked the same emergency provisions in a state of imminent threat of war as in a state of war. And the RS declared a state of imminent threat of war in April 1992. As Karadzic explained at the 50th Assembly, all the laws that would be invoked if a state of war were declared were already "fully in place." Except one: Court-martials with summary executions. That's at P4583 at pages 104 and 342. The absence of a declared state of war was not the result of its marginal to non-existent impact on the army but the perceived impact on the common purpose. As one VRS officer explained, the JCE members' motivation for not declaring a state of war: "It was their opinion at the time that if you are not in a war, then the laws of war do not apply." And making clear what he meant by referring to forced Muslim departures. That's P439, paragraph 5. The Defence also claimed that the Prosecution argued last week that Mladic and Drljaca, the Prijedor SJB chief, were "best buddies." The reality is that we mentioned Drljaca twice and cited his statement about exceptional co-operation between the VRS and the RS MUP. That doesn't mean we claim or rely on some sort of bromance between Drljaca and Mladic, but it is, of course, one of many reflections of the co-operation between the Prijedor SJB and the 43rd Brigade during the cleansing campaign. And for others, see P2432 and P4062, a note from Drljaca thanking 1 KK commander Talic for his "wholehearted help" during 1992. Despite the attempt by the Defence to create a straw man issue and knock it down, the VRS and the RS MUP are very much in it together. The Defence also suggested that we tried to recast some MUP perpetrators in Prijedor as VRS soldiers. The first example they gave was the unsuccessful attempt to prepare the camps for a visit by journalists, and they cited the alleged difference between our reference to Mladic's order to clean up camps and a question that, as it happened, I had asked a witness in the Brdjanin case about whether Zupljanin, the regional head of the MUP in the ARK, was involved. The next day of submissions, however, the Defence, with a straight face, showed the Court Mladic's order, P2879, and observed that Mladic was ordering Talic to take orders including through the MUP to get ready for the visits. Through the MUP in the ARK means through Zupljanin. So the VRS and the police again are just working together and there is no inconsistency in those questions. Mr. Ivetic's argument falls under its own weight. Now, the Defence next tried the same meritless claim about Omarska and Keraterm. And we are clear in our brief that Prijedor MUP officers commanded Omarska and Keraterm. See that at paragraph 537, paragraphs 33, 34, and 37 of the Prijedor narrative and in the Prijedor incident chart. We explain the VRS co-operated in running the camps, including providing security and interrogators and rounding up the people detained and abused there, but the MUP had primary responsibility and the commanders were MUP staff. We're clear about it and there is no inconsistency there. On Monday, the Defence cited a document that isn't in evidence, Security Council Resolution 752, which they claimed a reasonable person might find Zeljaja was "poorly effectuating," when he threatened to burn down Kozarac. But what is in evidence clearly exposes that this explanation is not capable of belief. P2052 shows that in Resolution 752 the Security Council had "demanded that all units of the JNA and elements of the Croatian army now in BiH must either withdraw, or be subject to the authority of the government of BiH, or be disbanded and disarmed with their weapons placed under effective international monitoring." And also see adjudicated fact 291. So the Security Council was not empowering Zeljaja to disarm anyone, let alone burn their villages to the ground if they did not obey him. It was saying he had to disarm, leave or put himself under the Bosnian Presidency's command. The evidence also shows in respect of that issue Zeljaja's demand that the residents of Kozarac surrender 7.000 weapons was just a pretext. Drljaca concluded at the same time that between Kozarac and Kozarusa all there was was a unit of "company strength"; P2869. And so accordingly, the 43rd Brigade, by that time part of the VRS, quickly and brutally cleansed the village, killing or removing civilians as well as soldiers, including women, children, and elderly. Incidentally, in addition to the Security Council resolution, the Defence has cited a number of documents in its brief and argument that simply are not in evidence. We identified those documents to them a few weeks ago but they haven't yet made those corrections. I presume they will so during surrebuttal. And in similar spirit, with respect to the citation to P7441 in footnote 304 of our Prijedor narrative, consistent with the Trial Chamber's decisions we do not rely on pages 15 through 20 of that document. Now, in contrast to the evidence outlined in our submissions concerning the JCE members' concerns about the prospect of Bosnian independence and their preparation to divide Bosnia by force, if necessary, the Defence in its submissions painted a picture of Bosnian Serbs threatened by a "monster"; the Islamic war machine, essentially the same as modern-day ISIS, led by the author of the "The Islamic Declaration," Izetbegovic, who sought Serb destruction, exemplified by the SDA mouthpiece magazine Vox and their purported calls for beheadings of Serbs and their welcoming of the Fourth Reich. Now although we know all far too well that there were many victims on all sides and perpetrators of all ethnicities, this apocalyptic depiction of the circumstances simply does not square with the evidence and cannot serve to insulate General Mladic from responsibility for his crimes. And by way of some examples, the evidence shows that: First, the supposedly galvanizing threat of the Islamic Declaration wasn't even mentioned at the Bosnian Serb Assembly until late 1993 and then in a manner that made it clear the Speaker wasn't sure anyone knew what he was talking about. Karadzic acknowledged during the election campaign that Muslims were Europeanized Slavs, not fundamentalist fanatics, with whom Serbs would always live. And after the elections, the three nationalist parties formed a coalition government. You can find those at P7759, pages 8 through 9; and P6921, page 13. Izetbegovic's intentions as seen by the Bosnian Serbs were also evidenced in a discussion between Koljevic and Tudjman in January 1992, P6727, which reveal Koljevic promoting ethnic homogeneity through population transfers in response to Izetbegovic's interest in a "civil state." Another example: Vox magazine was not advocating what was shown on the cover, dramatically shown on the cover, beheadings and the Fourth Reich -- and the welcoming of the Fourth Reich. They were denouncing it and condemning efforts to pit one people against another. After this monumental fuss made by the Defence, please read the introduction to the article, which shows just the opposite of what they claimed. That's D580, page 2. As for the Defence portrayal of the VRS as a ragtag army fighting a "monster," the "Islamic war machine," 1st Krajina Corps commander Talic before the VRS was established declared: "The Banja Luka Corps has such a large force and such an organisation that there is no risk of the corps or the people of Krajina being endangered," P7464, an assessment his Chief of Staff Kelecevic concurred with in testimony here, T37174. On the 23rd of May, 1992, the 1st Krajina Corps reported to Mladic that it was at 128 per cent of its establishment strength. P3987. Muslim forces in the charged municipalities by comparison were ill-equipped to contend with this powerful force as Defence witness Kupresanin acknowledged at the time, telling the Assembly in September 1992: "We had aviation, Howitzers, tanks, cannons, but what did the Muslims have? Some gun, some machine-guns they bought from Serbs, and homemade guns. We could have gone through Bosnia like a knife through cheese." Page 6291, page 10. That was because the Bosnian Serbs got the JNA's equipment at the transformation. So General Mladic wasn't a superman, as they claim. He was just a guy on a mission who had sufficient forces under his command to go through Bosnia like a knife through cheese and who used those forces to commit massive crimes and destroy communities. Internationals knew Bosnian government forces were no war machine. Wilson explained that as of May and June 1992, BiH forces were "not yet a complete fighting force. They were lightly equipped and had limited training. They had a way to go before they would be a competent military force." The SRK, on the other hand, was well equipped, well organised, and fought professionally. You find that at transcript 4008 through 4011. Mr. Weber cited last week the evidence that the SRK continued to be better-armed and equipped throughout the war. But let me simply refer to two days in the summer of 1992 which reflected the reality at the time. First a meeting of June 20, 1992, of the Bosnian Presidency, that's P7692, which reflects the Presidency members discussing what to do about Muslims being forcibly transferred by those "whose intention it is to create some ethnic territories, move the population, and to create clean national units." And reflects Izetbegovic noting their dilemma: "If we don't accept the ultimatum, these people really could be hurt. If we accept it, we're legalizing ethnic division; that is, the alteration of the demographic picture of Bosnia, the creation of ethnically clean territories." And then further noting that in any event: "Regarding all those agreements, I think they later simply point their cannons and kill all those people. Wherever they surrendered their weapons, et cetera, they ended up getting hurt." And that's at page 4 of the document. And another day in the summer of 1992, in July, at the Bosnian Serb Assembly, they are not discussing -- this is at the 17th Session, which is P4581. They're not discussing there the dilemma of accepting forcible transfer to avoid worse things happening. They are instead discussing things like Karadzic explaining how well the creation of the factual situation by Mladic is proceeding: "We have liberated almost everything that is ours in final talks, we could even return some territories, villages that do not belong to us." Other speakers chime in to praise Karadzic for visiting and inspiring them in driving the Muslims out of territories where they had actually been majority; that's page 65. Or expressing the hope that at least half the Muslims in Birac were gone; page 73. And Karadzic, referring to an earlier speaker who said that the Muslims had been planted to Serbs as a people whose executioners Serbs were to be, Karadzic agreeing that Europe drove them into the conflict "in order to eliminate the Muslims." Pages 41 and 86. The Defence also exaggerates the number of Muslims and Croats serving in the VRS, asking rhetorically whether Muslim and Croat VRS soldiers were committing genocide against their own people. Well, that's exactly why Muslim conscripts remaining in the VRS at that time asked to be released or deserted from their military units. They were "dissatisfied" with the massive destruction of their towns by VRS forces. That's P151. In order to hype the supposed number of non-Serbs in the VRS, the Defence cites data which includes Muslims and Croats who moved out of the area, who served in the JNA but never served in the VRS, and who served only after the war, while ignoring evidence of non-Serbs purged from the VRS. For that see paragraph 36 of our brief. In any event, Your Honours, the limited number of ethnic Muslim or -- Muslims or Croats who remained in or joined the VRS for whatever personal reasons does not gainsay the crimes or Mladic's responsibility. The Defence also claims that without the "shroud of a JCE" Mladic's meetings were "just the normal discussions between organs of a government ... engaged in a conflict." That might be true if one assumes that it is merely normal government business to discuss the fact that the army has fulfilled some, but not all, of the strategic objectives, and that it was time to ciscenje the Drina and achieve strategic objective number 3, a meeting that was followed by Mladic's Directive 4 to force the Muslim population out of the Drina area together with Muslim forces; that's P358, pages 146 through 147. Or assuming that it is normal government business when local authorities gather with their top leadership, including Mladic and Karadzic, to brag about the reductions of Muslim populations in places like Foca, Kljuc, Bratunac, Zvornik, and elsewhere. And that's cited in our brief, paragraph 290, for example. But beyond that, this is an example of how the Defence would like you to look at evidence in isolation. If Mladic and Mico Stanisic meet in July 1992 about co-operation between the VRS and the RS MUP, when you know from the totality of the evidence that the VRS and the MUP are -- doing together at the time includes running camps where non-Serb civilians are detained and abused and jointly conducting ethnic cleansing operations, then it isn't just a normal government meeting. It's a meeting between two people whose organisations are committing massive crimes together in order to fine-tune their co-operation. Because that is what the evidence in its totality tells you. The Defence's assertions that it isn't clear what the Prosecution case is about is grounded on obviously pretextual claims; for example, that we dropped the charges about Kalinovik municipality in closing argument by noting that Mladic had used Kalinovik's servile Muslims as an example of some Muslims who might not have to be removed while also pointing out that Mladic's subordinates later ethnically cleansed the municipality. General Mladic is charged with that cleansing as he has been throughout the trial. And in a similarly preposterous fashion, the Defence claim that because the first quote cited during our submissions was from 1993 when Mladic took credit for the cleansing his forces had led since 1992, they are somehow confused about the commencement date of the JCE, which is spelled out clearly in the indictment and no less clearly stated in our brief and in our submissions. Mladic is only charged with crimes after 12 May - see, for example, paragraph 191 of our brief - but evidence of what he and other JCE members did before that is relevant to the existence of the JCE and its objectives. He isn't charged for crimes in Croatia, but what he did there, as I explained earlier, helps to show his intent for the crimes he's charged with, Karadzic's intent, and the intent of other JCE members, like Milosevic, who oversaw the campaign in Croatia. This is no surprise, as you can see, for instance, in paragraph 15 of the Chamber's decision admitting the evidence of Milan Babic. The Defence also claims that they can't tell what specific criminal acts Mladic is charged with. But that ignores, for example, Annex B of the Prosecution's brief which identifies for the municipalities part of the case the evidence proving beyond a reasonable doubt the murders, destruction of cultural sites, detention and cruel treatment with which General Mladic is charged and for which we seek conviction. The crimes we refer to by name in Annex B are the same ones we charged in the indictment with one exception. Annex B shows we only seek convictions on two mosques in Kalinovik. We do not seek convictions on the mosques Mr. Riedlmayer did not conclude were destroyed during the war and which Mr. Ivetic referred to on Friday and we didn't include them in Annex B. Other persecutory acts, like dismissals and destruction of property are cited in Annex A. The Defence also referred to uncharged and dropped crimes, suggesting that their inclusion in the evidence can only reflect an intention to convict General Mladic for those crimes. Now this claim ignores the pleadings, the jurisprudence, and is not grounded on any position to that effect by the Prosecution. Simply put, the Chamber can and should consider such crimes helped prove the widespread and systematic attack on non-Serb civilians and the pattern of crimes Mladic and other JCE members used to ethnically cleanse the territories they claimed and their intent. We've given notice we would use pattern evidence this way throughout the trial. For instance, the Defence claimed we did not fulfil our obligation to give notice that we would lead evidence about dropped camps in Sanski Most, Sokolac, and Kotor Varos which formed part of the pattern of crimes against non-Serbs in those municipalities and which we cite in our brief. Well, first, we did give notice in our 65 ter list - see pages 90 through 95, 99 through 100, 124 through 125, 129 through 130, 171, 176 - that we would lead evidence about the camps in those municipalities, and, in any event, it wasn't an obligation. See transcript 9770 through 71. There are no surprises here. Just evidence so overwhelming that the Defence feigns confusion rather than engage with the case. The Defence suggested that our focus on Prijedor meant that we abandoned Count 1 for other municipalities. Now, in fact, we provided the analytical framework that the Chamber should apply to the facts of each charged municipality and said precisely that. But by way of example, as a result of a similar ethnic cleansing campaign conducted in Foca --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Tieger is not referring to our closing argument because we did not say that they had abandoned Count 1. We addressed Prijedor as Your Honours will recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The suggestion was, Mr. President, that the other charged municipalities -- that it was a concession by the Prosecution with respect to other charged municipalities. That's what I was referring to and that's what I'm addressing. So by way of an example of how to apply the analytical framework to the other charged municipalities as a result of a similar ethnic cleansing campaign to Prijedor that was conducted in Foca, which was geographically the largest municipality in Bosnia and a symbol to Serbs of Islam, General Mladic himself noted that Foca was 99 per cent Serb by September 1992. And using the facts detailed in the municipality summary, the Trial Chamber would consider the thousands of acts falling within Articles 4(2)(a) through (c), hundreds killed in KP Dom and others in the massacre at Trosanj. Serb forces rounded up Foca's Muslims and detained them in facilities where detainees were constantly subjected to prohibited acts falling within 4(2)(a) through (c). Routine beatings, detention in terrible and terrifying conditions, deprivation of food, heat, medical care. The detainees' vulnerability from detention and the crimes against them before they were rounded up exacerbating the destructive impact of the conditions in those camps. As one survivor of KP Dom put it: "The conditions at KP Dom were well calculated to cause fear and demoralisation; in my opinion, everything was planned systematically to destroy us both mentally and physically." That's RM046, P738, page 9. Serb forces, particularly TG Foca soldiers under Mladic's command, perpetrated brutal crimes of sexual violence against women and girls they were detaining in camps or enslaving in soldiers' homes where they repeatedly raped or sexually assaulted these victims, some over a period of many months. One survivor of the cleansing campaign in the camps observed: "I will not recover. My life was destroyed. My family was destroyed. The dearest to me were killed. All that I had in life, they took my happiness." RM070, T11752 through 753. And the Chamber will also assess the totality of the attack, including the traumatic forcible transfer and destruction of mosques, in assessing the destructive intent which is illuminated by the means chosen to achieve the objectives of the common purpose in Foca. The scale, level, brutality of the crimes illuminate Mladic's intent and the intent of other JCE members as do the repeated expressions of satisfaction by the Bosnian Serb leadership in the results of the cleansing campaign in Foca that we set out in paragraph 2 of the municipality summary. And all those factors and the totality of the evidence bearing on the assessment of destructive intent within the meaning of genocide convention in Article 4. The same analysis for each of the municipalities. Turning to Sarajevo for a moment, the Defence criticised the Prosecution for failing to mention Fadila Tarcin's testimony about where one of the shells came from during the G1 bombardment. They pointed to a limited portion of her testimony where she supposedly stated: "The shell came from the city, not from up the hill where the Serbs were." The Defence has yet again twisted the evidence. First, Tarcin testified that the shell impacted on the side of the house that faced the city. She did not say that the shell came from the city. That's T3447 through 48. More importantly, she testified at transcript 3424, and in her statement at P282, paragraph 3, that the shell came from Borije from the east of Sirokaca. The Chamber has ample evidence about the location of Borije which is located to the north-east and faces Sirokaca on the other side of the Miljacka river. In fact, SRK witnesses Veljovic - D532, paragraph 32, and T23002 through 23003, and 23013 - Dzida at D489, paragraph 17, and D490, paragraph 1 -- or page 1 - and Gengo, at transcript 21619, all confirmed that there were SRK positions, artillery positions in Borije. In addition to Sirokaca, the Stari Grad log-book, P549, page 72, also indicates other areas in Sarajevo, Vratnik and Kovaci, were targeted during G1 with projectiles coming from Borije. The Defence cited witness Oien to suggest the 28 June 1995 modified air bomb attack on the RTV building was fired by the ABiH and then cited Segers as having "confirmed that he knew of another instance where the same thing happened." The ABiH did not have modified air bombs. And the SRK boasted in an internal report about how they had hit the RTV building that day. That's D147. And UN reports confirmed the same thing; D165, pages 1, 6, and 12. And UNMO Brennskag even saw the modified air bomb fired from VRS territory fly through the air and strike the RTV building. That's P992, paragraph 52. Segers and Oien were clearly wrong. The Defence effort to convert Segers' testimony into a second event founders on the fact that Segers was talking about something he had only heard from a colleague in Zagreb a year later. Indeed, the Defence's extensive reliance on Segers' evidence collapses in the face of Segers' admission of serious memory issues and blackouts, and that he couldn't, in his own words, "really correctly even represent when I was in Sarajevo." That's T43803 through 04. At transcript 44745, the Defence argued that the ABiH was driven to shell and snipe their own people in order to perpetuate a myth that the SRK was doing this. In support they pointed to evidence of General Rose and Edin Garaplija. Rose, however, clearly acknowledged that while he was aware of such allegations in the media, he had no idea whether they were well founded or not; P736, paragraph 213. And other internationals such as Fraser were not even aware of such allegations, much less of evidence indicating that they had any basis. In any event, the insinuation that Rose was suggesting that the crimes for which Mladic stands accused were actually committed by the Muslim side inverts reality. Rose stated, in P736, paragraph 217, that "with respect to sniping, the level of sniping was definitely greater on the part of the Serbs" and "the greater number of civilians killed were obviously the Bosnians within the city of Sarajevo." The Prosecution addressed the widespread shelling of Sarajevo by the SRK in T44497 and 98 of its closing arguments and paragraphs 915 through 1002 in its final brief. As for Garaplija's claims, all based on the supposed confession of Nedzad Herenda. But Garaplija beat and tortured Herenda's confession out of him. Garaplija was sentenced to prison for the abduction of Herenda and the beating and shooting that occurred during this interrogation. Further, Garaplija's extravagant tales to justify his crimes as emerged on cross-examination have been repeatedly rejected through the years. No weight should be accorded his evidence. The Defence also claimed that modified air bombs were designed by experts with a detailed firing table which they claim the Prosecution denies in a "desperate attempt" to substantiate the allegations against Mladic. So let's scratch the surface a bit and see who's desperate. Although the Defence contends that the modified air bomb was not "amateurly designed," Milovanovic described it as a contraption that was "put together in a makeshift way," as was almost comically confirmed by Radojcic's admission that his own brigade, not a manufacturer, put together the rocket-launcher based on sketches from the superior command; T23044. And Radojcic's initial claim that there was a "firing table" turned out to be nothing more than his characterisation of a "temporary" or "provisional" piece of A4 paper with who knows - not him - what was on it; T23170. The only firing tables produced in connection with this issue which are not in evidence are for a Kosava rocket-launcher. In a 3 August 1995 order, P4282, General Mladic stated that the VRS "has a certain number of Kosava launchers from various manufacturers whose quality mostly does not ensure the necessary precision against FAB 105s [sic] or FAB 250s." In view of Mladic's contemporaneous acknowledgment of the imprecision, the development of firing tables that may have somehow improved the situation after the Scheduled Incidents does nothing to change the totality of evidence that the modified air bombs were a grossly imprecise weapon. And finally Veljovic, the Assistant Chief of Staff for operations and training for the SRK, testified that modified air bombs did not have firing tables and were widely known among the VRS as grotesquely inaccurate. That's T22949 to 53. Given the inherent inaccuracy and destructive capabilities of this weapon, it was a terrifying weapon for the Sarajevo population as Fraser, Konings, Radojcic, and Brennskag testified. At transcript page 44757, the Defence claim: "In fact, in accordance with their right to use force in self-defence, it was legitimate that the SRK would return fire in the face of an assault of [sic] their positions. Indeed, Witness Jordan confirmed such practice as standard operating procedure at transcript page 1818." In fact, Jordan did not confirm this. He said he didn't see a lot of it. But what he did say was that sniping civilians was part of "daily life," and that he "firmly believed" on the basis of observations from 1992 to 1995 that there was a deliberate attempt to terrorise the civilians of Sarajevo through shelling and sniping, recalling, among other things, how Serb shooters would go after the youngest person in a group; P126, paragraph 42. The Defence closing relied on Witnesses Segers and Mole to claim that the shelling of hospitals was really "return fire" that was "targeted technically at" mobile mortars but not the hospitals themselves; T44759. In fact, on the only occasion he saw a mobile mortar firing from somewhere on the Kosevo Hospital grounds, Segers saw that Serb artillery retaliated against the hospital building itself after the mobile mortar was gone; T43760 through 61. That is not "technically" targeting a mobile mortar. That is targeting a hospital. Apart from this one incident, Segers testified that he was regularly notified that the Kosevo Hospital was repeatedly and heavily shelled by VRS mortars and artillery. T43765. And Mole was explicit that the fire on the hospital was "retaliation, rather than a military response." P421, paragraph 126. You can find at paragraph 1042 of our brief references to the many reports and protests of the shelling of the hospital. See also paragraphs 1038 to 1041 regarding mobile mortars. Retaliation against civilian areas or objects is not a permissible response to attacks by mobile mortars. The Defence claimed during their submissions that the Prosecution "have seemed abjectly afraid" to talk about proportionality, suggesting that it is based on our "lack of any basic understanding of the principle." T44755. The Defence knows full well why proportionality is not the focus of discussion about the terror campaign, and that is because proportionality assumes an effort to hit a legitimate military target which then requires an assessment of the military value against the risk of collateral damage. That is not what happened. Instead, the SRK repeatedly fired at civilian areas or objects or included them in indiscriminate attacks. These are direct attacks on civilians that do not implicate proportionality. The Appeals Chamber in Dragomir Milosevic, paragraph 53, and Galic, paragraph 190, has emphasised that "it is well established that the principle of distinction requires parties to distinguish at all times 'between the civilian population and combatants, between civilian and military objectives, and accordingly direct attacks only against military objectives.'" Adding that: "There is an absolute prohibition against the targeting of civilians in customary international law, encompassing indiscriminate attacks." The existence of the proportionality principle does not save the SRK's campaign of sniping civilians and civilian objects, including women and children, buses and trams, from its abject illegality. It cannot justify single shells landing randomly across residential areas in the city centre where no military activity was occurring. It cannot justify treating the entire city as a target as the SRK did with massive bombardments like G1 and G2. It cannot justify repeated shellings of residential neighbourhoods. The Defence claims that indiscriminate bombardments such as G1 and G2 "are evidence of the SRK acting pursuant to their objective to bring a permanent resolution to the conflict in Sarajevo." Those claims are misguided. Setting aside the perversity of the suggestion that Mladic's retaliatory attempts to "drive them out of their minds," that's P105, is a benevolent and laudable act, it is once again a reflection of Mladic's disdain for the principle of distinction. And for the same reason, the frankly chilling Defence argument that "the city of Sarajevo itself consisted a valid military target in its entirety," must be decisively rejected. As the Milosevic Appeals Chamber held at paragraph 54, when considering a similar argument, "a general assertion that the attacks were legitimate because they allegedly targeted 'military zones' throughout the city is bound to fail." Can we move into private session very quickly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Further, Your Honours, the evidence just discussed also dispatches the Defence claim that no VRS officer ever testified about an illegal Mladic order. That no proportionality analysis informed the G1 bombardment is also reflected in the discussion at paragraph 932 of our brief, reflecting the distancing from this manifestly indefensible attack by JNA authorities who "wanted nothing to do with any responsibility for the attack on that night." T3971. Defence efforts at deflection reach another low point with their claim that Sarajevo was not an undefended city. And they make the same assertion for Srebrenica and for Kozarac. The Prosecution never asserted that Sarajevo was an undefended city and that consequently any shelling was illegal. But the Defence relies on twisted logic. If it was not prohibited to fire at all, then any and all attacks on Sarajevo are permitted. The Prosecution never asserted that the SRK could not use appropriate force against military targets in Sarajevo. But it was not permitted to engage in a sniping and shelling campaign against civilians. The Defence trots out the manifestly irrelevant undefended city argument because the evidence overwhelmingly shows that that is how General Mladic and the VRS conducted themselves, in Sarajevo and elsewhere, treating entire cities, villages, and hamlets as if they were military targets. Moreover, while the Defence tries to shift the blame to the ABiH, claiming that it failed to separate civilians from military objects and was using civilians as human shields, even if this were true in some instances, the law is clear and well settled. The failure of one party to discharge obligations to remove civilians to the maximum extent feasible from the vicinity of military objectives and to avoid locating military objectives within or near densely populated areas does not relieve the other party of its proportionality duties when launching an attack in response. Galic Appeals Judgement, 194; Trial Judgement, 61; and Milosevic Trial Judgement paragraph 949. Now as part of its attack, the Defence claim that "the tenacious efforts of the Prosecution to continually manipulate the evidence to prejudice Your Honours with misleading assertions of proof, that's reasonable doubt. And that was based on two examples. The first was that RM147's testimony on the SRK's use of snipers in Sarajevo had "fizzled and disappeared" because he was not a member of a sniper squad. No, first of all, in fact it was the Prosecution that clarified the witness's status and further -- once again in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So in fact, Your Honours, RM147 presented evidence that clearly supported and advanced the Prosecution's case, Defence hyperbole to the contrary. Further, his evidence on the SRK's use of snipers in the Grbavica area of Sarajevo was corroborated by the Defence's own witness, Maletic, who confirmed that there was a sniper squad in the SRK "battalion command, directly subordinated to the commander." That's D482, paragraph 31, and T21758. In fact, Maletic recognised the name of one of the snipers appearing on the list of SRK snipers in P6517 and confirmed that this individual attended morning meetings with battalion commanders and deputy commanders; T21756. Witnesses RM147 and 141 identified some of these same snipers appearing in P6517. Also, as stated in P2624, paragraph 93, "everybody in Grbavica knew who the snipers were, nobody tried to conceal that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you repeat the number where you were talking about some of these snipers appearing in P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 6517. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for more detailed evidence on this issue, I refer Your Honours to footnote 3601 in paragraph 838 of the Prosecution brief. Now the other Defence example of so-called tenacious efforts to continually manipulate, et cetera, et cetera, brings us to Srebrenica. The Defence pointed to P1500, Mladic's authorisation of five tonnes of diesel fuel for the Zvornik brigade to carry out "engineering works" which the evidence shows was the reburial operation. The Defence does not contest the document authorised fuel for the reburial operation - see paragraphs 3293 through 3304 of their brief, and in particular 3298 - but claim that the Prosecution conceded that the numbering 03/4 reveals that the document came from the operations administration and "did not have to come from Mladic." But there is no inconsistency here. First the Defence agrees that SR which we see in the document means in his own hand - that's T16302 and see also T34887 - and that documents from Mladic personally are frequently drafted by operations, since the Defence itself tendered documents they say came from Mladic that had the 03/4 operations administration number; see D187. And for other examples of operations drafting, see P4562, 1557 and 1677. In any event, in this example, P1500, it is clear that it came from Mladic. Look at P2131, a follow-up order to issue the five tonnes of fuel ordered in P1500, which expressly acknowledges that P1500 was "pursuant to the order of the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska." Scratching the surface of these two examples, among others, show just who is tenaciously misleading. On the basis of a few words by Major Franken to the Dutch Ministry of Defence, the Defence asserted that Franken concluded that the transportation process of the Muslim population from Potocari was "benign" and "not the deportation nor forcible transfer." But the Defence did not provide with you Major Franken's further description when asked if he believed the population had a realistic choice to stay in Srebrenica: "There was theoretically a choice. The choice is in being crowded in weather like that with no supplies, with no food, with no medical care, comes to the fact then die slowly or get out. If you call that a choice, they had a choice." And then asked whether -- "was the choice that you just outlined between dying slowly or getting out, was that what you meant?" Franken said: "That's what I meant, yes." Contrary to the Defence suggestion, Franken actually concluded what the totality of the evidence makes clear: There was no voluntary departure, no choice. Precisely as intended by Karadzic and Mladic in Directive 7. The Defence stated three times in their closing that Prosecution military expert Butler did not find "a single order of General Mladic ordering the Srebrenica killings." What Butler actually testified to was the following: "I have not come across a document by General Mladic specifically ordering the execution of prisoners." We would not expect Mladic or his Main Staff to be so bold as to write up orders to Krstic, Tolimir, Beara and others specifically ordering prisoners to be murdered, particularly given Mladic's presence on the ground. Those would be done orally. We do have clear evidence of some of his individual orders in furtherance of the murder operations. For example, his order to his men to separate able-bodied men in Potocari which he announced at the Hotel Fontana on 12 July. See our brief at paragraph 1172. The order on 13 July to Furtula to provide a unit to work for Beara. Paragraphs 1289 through 96. The 13 July oral order to Malinic to stop registering the many hundreds of prisoners at Nova Kasaba. Paragraph 1261 of our brief. The 16 July oral order to Keserovic to command the sweep operation and its written counterpart dated 17 July, in effect an order to kill any prisoners captured during the sweep operation. Paragraphs 1337 through 1340. And, as discussed, his 14 September order for fuel for the reburials. Paragraph 1384. The Defence also claimed that in paragraph 1116 of our final brief we presented a "new theory" on the meaning of the Krivaja 95 attack plan. That paragraph observes that the objective to reduce the Srebrenica enclave to its urban area was designed to force the population into the urban area of Srebrenica and thereby create impossibly overcrowded conditions, replicating the 1993 humanitarian disaster in Srebrenica. This so-called new theory has always been the Prosecution's position about the Krivaja 95 attack plan. It was first noted in our pre-trial brief at paragraph 208, stated in our opening statement at page 486 and again in our 92 bis submission at T20835 through 36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, rather than to draw your attention to the clock at the very end of the one and a half hours, I do it some 15 to 17 minutes before that, so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart is apprising me of the time, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I should have known that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Falsely portraying this Prosecution position as new is a misleading way to attack a conclusion the Defence is otherwise unable to challenge. The Defence also claimed that the Prosecution assertion that Mladic and Krstic had dinner together at the Hotel Fontana on 11 July after the meetings with DutchBat was made up by the Prosecution for the first time in closing and was "not referenced in their final brief nor in the evidence." That's incorrect. Please find reference to the evidence of the dinner in our final closing brief in paragraphs 1174 and 1219. Mladic and Krstic were together at the Hotel Fontana that night as can be seen on the video of the second Hotel Fontana meeting. They were both staying at the Hotel Fontana and had dinner at the hotel together in the same place where the meeting was held. See transcript 11160 through 62. And this is where Mladic made the decision to "separate the able-bodied men," either that very night or the next morning, prior to Mladic's announcement of that decision at the 10.00 a.m. Hotel Fontana meeting on the 12th of July. Your Honours, I began these submissions this morning with reference to the Defence accusations against Prosecution and others which went so far as Mr. Lukic's insinuation about a trial process that brought to mind the "Fourth Reich." So let's look for just moment at the Fourth Reich trial that the Defence claims General Mladic received. We're now four and a half years past opening statements. In that time, the Chamber has heard almost 400 live witnesses, more than half called by the Defence. The Defence has spent almost 700 hours questioning witnesses in court. More time than the Prosecution, more time than the Chamber. They've admitted more than 2.000 exhibits into evidence, including three which the Chamber admitted this Monday, months after the deadline, just to make sure that Mladic had every chance to be heard on sentencing. And the trial stalled for half a year to allow them to call their last six witnesses, and when briefs were filed it was ten months after we'd regularly been in court. And until last Monday, we'd only spent 18 days in court, a lavish amount of time and opportunity for preparation of briefs and submissions. With that time, all those witnesses, all that evidence, they're left with hyperbolic arguments because the evidence of guilt is overwhelming. And while we're discussing Defence complaints about trial, recall that Mr. Ivetic argued - just one page before claiming that General Mladic felt sorry for the victims of the war - that "the Prosecution was allowed to eavesdrop on his communications with counsel." That's at T44832. A listener could have been forgiven for thinking that this related to trial strategy, what witness to call, what question to ask, some hushed conversation with counsel. Instead what Mr. Ivetic was referring to was Mladic during a court break, with Prosecution members in their normal place on the other side of the courtroom, loudly expressing ugly and ethnically charged insults about a Muslim woman witness who had survived terrible crimes of sexual violence. This wasn't about eavesdropping, this wasn't about trial strategy, and it wasn't about remorse. Finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic should not speak aloud. Mr. Mladic, if you continue to speak aloud, you know what the consequences will be. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Defence has argued repeatedly that General Mladic is on trial just because he is a Serb, asking why we did not charge international negotiators such as Akashi, Cutileiro, Owen, Stoltenberg, who at times reluctantly considered separation a solution, or the United Nations forces, some of them Dutch, who requested his permission to transport Muslims out of the Srebrenica enclave. Now, first, we set out for in paragraph 283 of our brief how the ethnic cleansing campaign presented internationals with an agonizing choice because they recognised that saving people from the persecution they were facing in their homes by evacuating them would in fact advance the Bosnian Serb policy of ethnic cleansing, but sometimes circumstances were so desperate that they had no choice. Srebrenica is a particularly chilling example. But more fundamentally, Ratko Mladic is not charged with thinking that ethnic separation is the best solution in a bad situation. He is charged with using the VRS to achieve it through the commission of brutal crimes. Ambassador Akashi did not lead an army which burned, raped, murdered, and pillaged its way through Serb-claimed territory, destroying Muslim and Croat villages and killing or expelling their residents. Ratko Mladic did. Ambassador Cutileiro did not order his subordinates to force Muslim civilians out of Eastern Bosnia. Ratko Mladic did. Ambassador Hurd did not order a subordinate to shell civilian areas in Sarajevo until its residents were driven out of their minds. Ratko Mladic did. Ambassador Owen did not order the use as hostages of hundreds of peacekeepers. Ratko Mladic did. Ambassador Stoltenberg did not order and oversee an operation in which 7.000 men and boys were executed. Ratko Mladic did. General Mladic is not on trial because he is a Serb. He is not on trial because he's a military officer. He's on trial because the evidence shows - and proves beyond a reasonable doubt - that he is guilty of crimes against humanity, war crimes, and genocide. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Lukic, would you, during the break, make clear to Mr. Mladic that we'll not allow any further loud speaking under the present circumstances. And, as Mr. Mladic knows, the ultimate consequences would be that he will be removed from the courtroom. We'll take a break. We'll take a break of half an hour, which we usually do if we have sessions of one hour and a half, and we'll resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume. Mr. Ivetic, your one and a half hour will start in a second. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will try to address as much as possible that which we have just heard from the Prosecution but I may not get to everything. I may not cover every little point, and I may not go into every little detail because we had a short time to process and prepare a response. But I will begin by addressing what Mr. Tieger called hyperbolic arguments. Your Honours, I don't think I need to remind you, but I will anyway, we have filed a final trial brief which is in excess of 900 pages. Within those 900-plus pages, we have gone through considerable detail making our arguments, addressing the Prosecution evidence, and giving citations to the evidence which we believe demonstrate reasonable doubt. It took Mr. Tieger one and a half hours to get to the point of just stating that the Prosecution had proven their case beyond a reasonable doubt, but they haven't demonstrated how they have done so. I would stress that Your Honours keep in mind what I said the other day when we went through the examination of the burden of proof and the appropriate standard. It's not just beyond a reasonable doubt, for we also have to keep in mind in dubio pro reo, which means that all inferences available under the evidence must be taken in favour of the accused. What the Prosecution would have you do is at all times take the inference in favour of the Prosecution by viewing the evidence in a vacuum. Your Honours, you cannot do that. Your Honours, the Defence has always asked you to look at the totality of the evidence and we stand behind that. The totality of the evidence, we submit, demonstrates that the Prosecution has failed to meet their burden when viewed under in dubio pro reo and all the other applicable legal principles. Now let me start off talking about JCE for a bit. Mr. Tieger mentioned today that 1991 in Croatia are not part of the case. Indeed they are not part of the indictment, that's for sure. But this Prosecution has led considerable evidence relating to 1991, relating to Croatia, and wants you to draw from that inferences and conclusions as to intent, wants you to draw from that evidence as to the existence of a JCE. And although Mr. Tieger was clear today for the first time that the criminal responsibility of the accused starts on 12 May 1992, we still didn't hear from them when it is alleged that this JCE came into existence and wherein Mr. Mladic agreed to join or participate in any JCE. In relation to 1991 in Croatia, which they've asked you to take into account and consider, the Prosecution have cited evidence from Ambassador Okun which was submitted under Rule 92 quater. We counted 12 citations within their final brief for which Okun's evidence is uncorroborated: Footnotes 632, 635, 642, 643, 1125, 1455, 1575, 1583, 1913, 1914, 1953, and 2847. They further referenced the testimony of Mr. Okun five times during closing arguments the other day; at transcript pages 44354, 44366, 44368, 44369, and 4470. Uncorroborated evidence admitted pursuant to Rule 92 quater in accordance with the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, such as the Milosevic [sic] case in volume 3, paragraph 276 of the Trial Judgement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the last reference to a page number, you said 4470. I assumed you meant 44370; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 44470, I omitted a 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I see the transcript has referenced the Milosevic case. I'm referencing the Milutinovic case, so I must have misspoken. In the Milutinovic case, it has been held that uncorroborated evidence admitted pursuant to Rule 92 quater is such that it's unable to rely upon that type of evidence to determine the acts and conduct of the accused. But that's what Mr. Tieger asked you to do just today. Why? Why didn't they bring more evidence? Why didn't they identify 1991 in Croatia in the indictment and have a fair and full adjudicated trial on that? They choose to do it this way. Now, while addressing the alleged overarching JCE, both in these past few days and in their final brief, the Prosecution has relied heavily on statements of politicians at the Assembly sessions which are taken out of context. An example is P4580, where General Mladic is not even present. In fact, for many of the items where the Prosecution is referencing other people, usually politicians, talking about things, General Mladic is not present, and yet they wish to attribute those words and derive intent from those words against General Mladic. I ask you, Your Honours, as I ask the world: Is that fair? At transcript page 44358, the Prosecution said: "The leadership considered that they had achieved the quality that is ethnic division and the destruction of Bosnia and so all that was left was a question of quantity," and they cited P4580. But if you look at the totality of the context, the discussion in question is a conference on solutions for the crisis in BiH; page 16 of that document indeed reflects as follows: "The value of this document is that it reflects what we have accomplished but is not final or complete. We believe that we shall achieve what was contested the most and that is a quality issue. The quality we want to achieve is having three BHs. What remains is a question of quantity which includes the issues of federation and confederation. How many functions will belong to the constituent state and how many to joint services." Your Honours, what the politicians were discussing was a continuation of how to bring about what existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina before the outbreak of hostilities, where all three ethnic parties had representative equal say in the governing of that republic per the constitution. And so even in the very document that the Prosecution cites that the Serb side wanted separation, they're still talking about how the three ethnic parties can live and work together in some sort of federation or confederation. They're just trying to restore the existing -- pre-existing constitutional order. Now, other examples where the OTP has relied upon statements of others taken out of context and tries to attribute them to Mladic are P3076, in relation to Karadzic; P406, also in relation to Karadzic; P6997, in relation to Brdjanin; P6994, in relation to Brdjanin; P3959, in relation to Brdjanin; and P4581, in relation to Plavsic and Koljevic. Now, today we heard Mr. Tieger talk about Karadzic and how -- how we were trying to deflect from damaging evidence and the reason that they cite to Karadzic is because he is a key partner of Mr. Mladic. Your Honours, we heard scarcely a word from Mr. Tieger addressing the arguments that we made that there wasn't a good relationship between Karadzic and Mladic at times, so how could they be working together as key partners in a criminal endeavour when they don't share similar views and had various conflicts? P2471, a Prosecution exhibit, it's alleged to be a conversation between Mladic, Karadzic, and Milovanovic, and this exhibit contains a conversation between Mladic and Karadzic which is quite argumentive, mainly at the end of page 1 and page 2 of that document. We have P1052, another Prosecution exhibit, extracts from an interview of an individual, and it specifies that: "There were personal misunderstandings between Karadzic and Mladic. The former represented the supreme authority and the latter did not like superiors, especially when they were not professionals but prone to meddling in his profession." We also have P736 at paragraphs 211 to 212, General Rose: "The relationship between General Mladic and Dr. Karadzic was as one would expect in a confused and brutal situation of varying intensity. At times, Mladic would appear to dominate the discussions and determine the course of events. On other occasions, Karadzic would be able to hold his political position and Mladic would then conform to that, depending very much on how pressed they felt, either politically or militarily on the ground." D862, the sworn statement of Witness Milutinovic, paragraph 130: "As I recall, the first disagreements and conflicts between General Mladic and President Karadzic as the supreme commander occurred in August 1993, when the supreme commander ordered the army to withdraw from Mount Igman and to hand over the position it had taken to UNPROFOR." Paragraph 132: "The conflict between General Mladic and President Karadzic emerged, inter alia, because the army personnel were hungry while there were war profiteers around them who used the war to become rich." Paragraph 138: "Bearing in mind the increasing divisions of the VRS between the supporters of Mladic and the supporters of Karadzic." We will stress yet again that in relation to our submissions if they were key partners, why did President Karadzic try to remove General Mladic on multiple occasions? Surely the evidence does not support the assertion of the Prosecution that they were key partners. As to JCE, the Prosecution has alleged that Alija Izetbegovic's the Islamic Declaration was not known, I guess they mean to say that people didn't really care about it, but we had evidence to the contrary. The Bosnian Serb leaders were very aware of the Islamic Declaration and were quite concerned about what it meant. We had Witness Dodik testify at transcript page 42267, when questioned whether the declaration was discussed at Assembly sessions: "We had in mind what was Alija Izetbegovic's policy in 'The Islamic Declaration,' which I, myself, read several times ... and I think that any man who was involved in any degree in politics at the time was aware of the contents of this declaration ... and it was nothing secret. It was a published document ... it became more popular than ever among his supporters." We have other evidence indicating the prominence of the Islamic Declaration and the fears generated by the same. We have transcript page 29633 to 29639, Witness Kupresanin; transcript page 23904, Witness Kecmanovic. We even have a Prosecution exhibit from a Prosecution witness, P3265. That was Witnesses MacLeod. And we also have a Defence Witness, Tadic, talking about that in his Defence statement, D661, paragraph 17. So to say that the Islamic Declaration was not in the minds of everyone, that's not -- that's not in accord with the evidence. Also, we have to take into account what happened afterwards because the book was published, the book called for a Jihad, it called for Bosnian Muslim dominance over others, non-believers. But that wasn't the end of it, and let's talk about this Vox article that Mr. Tieger references. And, yes, the authors of that article in Vox did a very clever thing by trying to say, Oh, we're going to publish this but we don't know where it comes from, it might have come from the Serbs. Well, that position is nothing more than them covering for their own deeds. And here's why. Tongue in cheek they could say that, but in addition to the pamphlet that's published, Vox made its own cover. Its own cover had a Bosnian Muslim Handzar Division soldier standing over the severed heads of Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, and other Serb leaders dressed up with Chetnik hats. The Serbs didn't make that up. There was the other article from Vox which was obituaries for the prominent Bosnian Serb political leaders at that time, all of whom were alive. The Serbs didn't make that up either. It is more likely under the evidence that the Bosnian Muslim leadership through Vox -- and we heard Vox was closely connected to the SDA and to the mayor of Sarajevo and to Alija Izetbegovic. What kind of message, as a Serb in Bosnia-Herzegovina, can you infer from the fact that all of a sudden you wake up and you no longer have your constitutional right as an equal partner in Bosnia and the other two parties can declare independence and address your fate? How do you feel when you read Alija Izetbegovic call for a Jihad? How do you feel when obituaries are published for Serbs before they are even dead? Well, one way that can be read and interpreted is fear. And we had a lot of evidence of fear felt by ordinary Serbs as a result of what was being published, what was being seen, and their memories of what had happened to them in the Second World War. In relation to JCE, and we had a reference to that today when Mr. Tieger talked about how the intent can be drawn from various documents talking about ciscenje of the Drina, and, again, the Prosecution likes to use a term that has a very specific, non-criminal, military meaning and tries to give it some sort of nefarious alternative meaning which fits their story. But we've had clear evidence of military expert Kovac at transcript page 41924 giving the definition of ciscenje in military terminology. Clearing or cleansing as is a concept that means searching the terrain for armed enemy formations in the area of responsibility or in the area of actions or the area of employment of forces, so within one's own disposition or in the area of use of forces, and it pertains to armed units. When asked about if there's any difference between ciscenje and ciscenje terena, or clearing of the terrain, Witness Kovac said "ciscenje" is a general term, whereas clearing the terrain means in fact pertaining to armed elements, armed unit, terrorists, sabotage groups, et cetera. That's what cleansing or clearing the terrain would mean. And in that regard, Your Honours, I would also point out that RM097 clearly distinguished between JNA orders for ciscenje and the forced removal of civilians or mistreatment of civilians. And thus, the use of ciscenje in military documents cannot be misinterpreted and given this nefarious meaning the Prosecution would like to give it. Now, the Prosecution spent some time talking about Foca, and, in particular, they focused upon the destruction of mosques in Foca. And, again, Your Honours, bearing in mind the burden of proof, bearing in mind that all inferences must be made in favour of the accused, we urge you to look at that evidence in its totality. Read it, analyse, and look for alternative explanations why or how those mosques in Foca might have been destroyed. Recall that we had a photograph of a military gun near the roof of a mosque. Recall that we had evidence of various witnesses talking about combat activities being undertaken by armed units of the ABiH from mosques. D706, Witness Trivko Pljevalcic, paragraph 8: "I was wounded on 14 July 1992. Concerning the fighting in the town of Foca itself, it lasted for some ten days. Ever since the conflict broke out, all our activity focused on defending or reacting to the Muslim forces' attacks. Our first casualty happened on the first day of the fighting, and he was killed by fire opened from the minaret of the Aladza mosque. I know the Muslim forces used their religious facilities for military purposes. They carried out training and stored weapons in them." And then paragraph 9: "As far as I know, the first fighter to be killed in Foca was Radoljub Trifkovic. He was the one who was shot from the Aladza mosque. I was some 10 metres from him when it happened. Dragan Nikolic was killed on that occasion as well." Then we had the testimony of Witness Vujicic. First at page 2420 of the transcript: "So when the Muslims procured arms and imported weapons into Foca, they predominantly put them in some places of worship. Some, not all. This is where they stored their weapons, the explosive substances and such-like. Furthermore, in parallel, in some of those facilities, such as the Pilav mosque in Gornje Polje, they trained the Green Berets and their armed forces and the Patriotic League." Transcript page 24201. Judge Orie asked the question at line 4: "Yes, because now you're explaining to us that activities took place in those mosques but the question was: When and in what manner were the mosques destroyed or damaged? That was the question. Can you please focus on that. "The Witness: [Interpretation] These mosques were demolished for the most part in conflicts, in combat activities, precisely because the Muslims opened fire from the minarets of some of these mosques. Personally, I personally could see Muslims shelling Serb positions and Serb houses from some mosques. And then, on the other hand, later, sometime in 1995, after the NATO forces fired several projectiles on Foca, these mosques, as very old buildings, were damaged considerably and demolished. This is how these places of worship came to be destroyed." Again, Your Honours, you have to look at the totality of the evidence. When an alternative explanation for a fact is seen, you have to take the one that is giving credit to the accused. And as to these mosques in Foca -- which is not to say that this is what happened to mosques elsewhere, you have to look at every municipality based upon its evidence and what was presented. But as to Foca, we have this evidence which the Prosecution has not addressed and which provides an alternative explanation under which General Mladic is not responsible and, therefore, cannot be criminally responsible for the same. In relation to something that Mr. Tieger brought up near the end of his presentation today, he seemed to take offence at my use of the term "eavesdropping" to describe what his staff did when they testified about statements made between General Mladic and his attorneys, and he claimed that it occurred because Prosecution staff just happened to be where they were supposed to be and they heard things. But he didn't address how Prosecution staff came to that position that they were at, and I take great offence at his representations in that regard because he is hiding that the Prosecution counsel instructed that staff to be there and instructed them to be able to listen in precisely on the privileged communications of the accused and his counsel. For a fellow lawyer to stand up and say what Mr. Tieger said makes me sick. Similarly, at transcript page 18174, one of those Prosecution staff members, Witness Sokola, specifically identified that Prosecution counsel in this case tasked them with noting down everything that Mladic said, even private affairs. That's at transcript page 18174. At transcript page 18180, that same witness confirmed that all of the communications were between Mladic and his Defence attorneys, not with anyone else. When asked about how they came to be there, at 18172 the witness identified that they were specifically tasked with staying in the courtroom with the express purpose of listening in on the conversations. And when asked if it was pointed out to them by Prosecution counsel that communications between a defendant and their counsel is privileged, the witness stated it was not pointed out to her at that time. So we have a Prosecution office that sees no problem with destroying attorney/client privilege. I ask you, Your Honours, I ask the world: Is that fair? Is that how we want trials to be run by a Prosecution? Now I'd like to move to Sarajevo. To begin with, it appears based upon today's presentation that the Prosecution has conceded proportionality and now focuses only on selectively. At temporary transcript page 23, lines 6 through 9, Mr. Tieger said: "The Defence knows full well why proportionality is not the focus of the discussion of the terror campaign, and that is because it assumes an effort to hit a legitimate military target which then requires an assessment of the military value against the risk of collateral damage." Well, Your Honours, we submit proportionality must be and is required by law to be viewed to assess military action such as shelling. We talk about -- or they talked about G1, a shelling campaign, which, by the way, apart from Ms. Fadila Tarcin, I ask you have they identified and brought any other alleged casualty from G1? They keep talking about a lot of casualties but where's the evidence of that? How can we defend against unknown casualties, unsubstantiated claims of casualties? But let's talk about the evidence that exists of military targets of the ABiH side, legitimate military targets, that were the target of the selective fire that was engaged in G1. As to Bascarsija, we have D802. As to Velesici, we have D653. As to Vratnik, we have P549. And as to Sirokaca, D524. So if their claim is that there were no military targets, that isn't supported by the evidence. There is an alternative conclusion. Now, furthermore, as to Sirokaca we have something more and I want to address that next. Ms. Fadila Tarcin, is it really the Defence that is misrepresenting her testimony? Rather than have you stand on my words, I will read to you from the transcript of Witness Fadila Tarcin's words and you can assess for yourselves, as the whole world can assess, whether I am being faithful to those words or whether, as Mr. Tieger said, we're the ones misrepresenting them. And again this is a Prosecution witness. Transcript page 3424 [Realtime transcript read in error "3242"]: "Q. Thank you, madam, and I appreciate that. Now, in this paragraph, you also state: "'According to the locals, the shell came from Borije to the east of us.'
