utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to Sarajevo, the Prosecution claimed that you don't need to look at defended city because the Prosecution never once talked about Sarajevo being an undefended city. Well, on the one hand, that's Mr. Tieger's way of admitting that Sarajevo was a defended city but trying to wiggle away from what that means under the law and it is very critical. But before we get there, I'm surprised that Mr. Tieger does not know what his very own indictment alleges because it is very clear as to Counts 9 and 10 as to Sarajevo, Count 6 as to murder, that these charges are brought pursuant to Article 3 of the ICTY Statute. And, Your Honours, if you remember when I read the other day and when Mr. Tieger asked what Statute, what Statute, I read from the ICTY Statute, which in Article 3, which the Prosecution cites in their indictment, clearly says that the violations that are being prosecuted against relate to attacks or bombardments by whatever means of undefended towns, villages, dwellings, or buildings. Hence, the Prosecution did explicitly indicate for Counts 9 and 10 and 6 that those localities were undefended which they have now conceded is not the case. Acquittal, Your Honours. Defended city applies not just to Sarajevo. It applies to Srebrenica. It applies to every single locality in the municipalities wherein there was an armed military force that was posing a defence of that locale and refused to render the city an open city. Now, let's look at the law. What is an undefended city? Article 59(2), Additional Protocol I, says an undefended city is an inhabited place near or in a zone where armed forces are in contact which is open for occupation by an adverse party. If there is no agreement in place, the following four conditions must also be met. All combatants, mobile weapons, and mobile military equipment have been evacuated. Was that Sarajevo? No. Was that Srebrenica? No. Was that those villages in the municipalities that had ABiH units situated within them or armed Bosnian Muslim paramilitaries within them? No. The second condition is no hostile use is made of fixed military installations or establishments. Was that Sarajevo? No. Was that Srebrenica? No. No acts of hostility are committed by the authorities or by the population. And, 4: No activities in support of military operations are undertaken. Commentary to AP I, Article 59, states roads and railways passing through the non-defended locality must not be used for the movement of combatants or military equipment, not even for transit purposes. Recall the tunnel in Sarajevo. Recall the existence of ABiH forces in Sarajevo. And Article 59(6), Additional Protocol I, there must be signs in place for the undefended city. You will recall the testimony as to Srebrenica, for instance, that there was not any signs marking the alleged demilitarised zone. Now, if we look at the BiH military instructions of 1992, even they concede for a locale to be undefended it has to either be recognised by the parties or fulfil certain conditions, including lack of a defence or armed forces, lack of military units for the purpose of transporting military material, lack of activities of a military importance, lack of a liaison with local armed forces and allied armed forces. The SFRY military manual from 1988 says that an undefended locale must be in accord with the New Delhi draft rules of 1956. When a locality is declared to be an open town, the adverse party shall be notified. "The latter is bound to reply, and if it agrees to recognise the locality ... as an open town ... in the absence of special conditions which may, in any particular case, be agreed upon with the adverse party, a locality, in order to be declared an 'open town,' must satisfy the following conditions: It must not be defended or contain any armed force; it must discontinue all relations with any national or allied armed forces; it must stop all activities of a military nature or for a military purpose ... it must stop all military transit through the town." Now, Your Honours, we have at various times in the case talked about defended city. We've presented military manuals of the UK and the United States that show this vision of what is an undefended city and therefore not a legitimate target and what is a defended city and is a legitimate target, under SFRY law complies with what all armies in the world likewise agree with. So, in our submissions, Sarajevo, for instance, is not an undefended locale. It is a defended locale. We have multiple military targets that are in Sarajevo that are legitimate to be selected for fire. We have, for instance, significant ABiH deployment through the neighbourhood of Hrasnica, including the forward command post of the 104th Brigade at Hrasnicki Stan; D559, paragraph 2. We also have the ABiH special forces training centre at Alekse Santic school; D559, paragraph 21. Two sky-scrapers, and there were machine-guns in place in one flat a couple of stories under that or above that were families living. Colonel Sekovac testified as to that, transcript page 24036. And D559, paragraph 19, talks about the post office in Hrasnica being used for military purposes. As to Sokolje, two trailer-trucks loaded with dynamite were located at Sokolje; D2015, page 2. As to Alipasino Polje, we have information that a very large number of Green Berets are inside the Sarajevo RTV building every day. There are 50 to 70 of them at a given time. D2015, D453, Witness Sladoje. We heard that the agricultural complex also had military activities; T21067. Dolac-Malta near the Geodetski Zavod, the Geodesic Institute, P468, paragraph 9; the Unis sky-scraper, D647; the ZIS, D647; the Sibica sky-scraper, D647; and the Vaso Miskina school, D489, paragraph 13. In Dobrinja, there were mortars positioned in the park approximately 500 to 700 metres from the front line; D559, paragraph 20. In Nedzarici, the Oslobodjenje newspaper building was used by the ABiH. We have that at D453. In Otoka, the Miljacka building was used; P647. In Kosevo, the home for deaf and impaired of hearing children at Fuada Midzica Street, a major communications centre was placed there on purpose by the ABiH; D647, page 2. The special unit of the CSB Laste was stationed in a catering establishment just opposite to the Olympic museum; D647, page 2. The psychiatry clinic was used; D647, page 3. The faculty of physical education was used; Witness Rasevic, D551. Kosevo stadium, Kosevo Hospital, Kosevo Brdo tunnel, and the Nemanja Vlatkovic school were likewise used by the ABiH; D551. In Bjelave, the trade school as well as the students' hostel compound were used; D647. In Cengic Vila, the Silvije Strahimira Kranjcevic elementary school was used by HVO members; D647, page 2. We had the Zrak factory in Buca Potok; D647. The Jewish cemetery in Kovacici and Soukbunari; D4849. We have several maps in evidence, D469 and D470, for instance, which talk about military targets that were positioned therein. I could read a very long list but we have evidence all over the place talking about military targets that are in Sarajevo that are actively firing upon the Serbs. No, Your Honours. Sarajevo is the textbook example of a defended city which becomes a legitimate target because the ABiH has taken actions to place its forces near civilians to use them as civilian shields. Therefore, proportionality must be a part of our discussions, unlike what the Prosecution said in their presentations. I remind Your Honours that the SRK was careful not to engage civilians or civilian targets which had been confirmed as such by visual observations or information gathered from informants and persons who had fled Sarajevo. Witness Tusevljak testified about that at transcript page 38460. We further have D535, paragraph 136; D824; D825; D643; D540; D468; D658.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, selectivity was at the forefront of the targeting of the SRK. We heard Mr. Tieger say that General Mladic had an army that could cut through Bosnia like a knife through cheese. But it didn't. It didn't take Sarajevo. It didn't try to take Sarajevo. It fought a defensive war, defending against attacks of the ABiH from the city itself. Now, commentary as to Article 52(2) of the Additional Protocols of the Geneva Conventions at 2024 talks about definite military advantage that can come from the destruction, capture or neutralisation. 2025 talks about a specific area can constitute a legitimate military objective in view of its location and the circumstances. This is commentary from Canada, Federal Republic of Germany, the Netherlands, and the United States. And the United Kingdom made a similar statement in a plenary meeting and repeated this in a written declaration when signing the Additional Protocols. Proportionality in the context of an attack on a defended town or locale must be considered in the context of the conflict as a whole. Bombardments are acceptable. See our information in the closing arguments in relation to this heavy shelling. I would also point out that several witnesses talked about this in court. Go look back at Piers Tucker, General Fraser, Witness Butler, and Witness Kovac, who talked about the defended city doctrine in very clear terms and, for instance, discussed overwhelming force doctrine, which it was argued by I believe it was Mr. Tucker that the NATO commanders who were in charge of doing the bombings against the Serbs were so tied up in their vision of overwhelming force as taught under NATO doctrine that they didn't want to use restraint against the Serbs. There's no discussion of that by the Prosecution. They would say that that doesn't exist. You have to always use restraint. Well, if NATO can do something, the Serbs do less than NATO does and they show restraint, why are they guilty? Again, it's the Serbs not NATO doing it. That's the Prosecution's case. There is a military strategy called shock and awe. It's tied to overwhelming force. It's based on achieving rapid dominance over the adversary by an initial imposition of overwhelming force and fire-power. Rather than focusing solely on defeating the military capability of an adversary, shock and awe or rapid dominance has the goal of affecting the adversary's will beyond boundaries traditionally defined by military capability and does not rely on military superiority. Did the Serbs try to end the war early and therefore limit casualties on all sides with G1? Let's recall the evidence also shows that when G1 was started it was -- it was then cancelled as they saw that too much of a risk of civilian damage existed, and then Karadzic said to stop that activity. So selectivity was at the forefront of the minds of the SRK as they were doing their activities around Sarajevo. Article 3 of the Statute says you can't bomb an undefended town, village, dwelling or building. It must be interpreted in light of customary international law which arguably says you can bomb a defended town, village, dwelling or building. Manual -- military manuals around the world distinguish between each of these features or use the word "locality." The importance of this is that each distinguishes between buildings, villages, towns, and dwellings. And bombardments against these towns and localities is therefore subject only to the normal criteria for engaging a target. It must be a valid military target and the attack must be proportionate. The mere fact there were civilians in Sarajevo doesn't mean it wasn't a valid military target. It just means it has to be treated as a military target with the civilians taken into account and given consideration as to proportionality, and this was done. Prosecution has not shown that attacks on Sarajevo were disproportionate in these regard. Other reasons why -- strike that. As to Sarajevo, we have to stress again that under the Gotovina case law, the Appeals Chamber at paragraph 66, we stress that the very presence of mobile mortars in Sarajevo calls in question the Prosecution's allegation that the SRK fired indiscriminately, and again the Gotovina Appeals Chamber at paragraph 66 said that the presence of mobile mortars "raises reasonable doubt whether even artillery impact sites particularly distant from fixed artillery targets considered legitimate ... demonstrate that unlawful shelling took place." Given the biases of international witnesses who were not in a position to judge the fire of the SRK as indiscriminate, this undermines their assertions about both the origin and impact of the artillery and small-arms fire in Sarajevo. At paragraph 79 of the Gotovina Appeals Judgement, it was effectively held that the observations of witnesses with no artillery experience and whose vantage points made it difficult to determine where the shells were directed at or actually landed was not sufficient to base a finding that the shelling was indiscriminate. Your Honours, the same applies to this Prosecution's evidence as to Sarajevo. The Gotovina and Markac Appeals Judgement says that you can't apply strict liability. You can't say that any shell that lands more than 200 metres from a military target was indiscriminate because that doesn't take into account such things as wind, temperature, and distance. That's at paragraph 60 to 61 of that Judgement. Now let's talk about what I said before, where is the evidence of any victims of G1 proven beyond a reasonable doubt? The Prosecution has presented P7171, a report which is a list of people that died on a day, 15 November 1993. There's no evidence as to how they died. No evidence linking them to G1. No evidence that they were in civilian locations as opposed to being unfortunate civilians held hostage by the ABiH who would have put their positions in their midst. There is no evidence that these victims are even civilians. They could be combatants. Another Prosecution Exhibit, P7731, says six people died in the latest barrage. Again, no identification for these six victims of any of these factors. And, again, despite all this talk of casualties, the Prosecution brought Fadila Tarcin and insists on using Fadila Tarcin to try to meet the onerous burden of proof. They can't get to the top of the pyramid, Your Honours. Not with that evidence. Now with regard to modified aerial bombs, Mr. Tieger pointed to various evidence and he mentioned Witness Radojcic. Let's recall that Witness Radojcic appraised the modified aerial bombs as being quite accurate. As Mr. Tieger even conceded, the testimony of Mr. Radojcic says that his unit prepared the launcher based upon schematics, drawings. They didn't just put something together without expertise. They had a document how to use it. Mr. Tieger focused on Mr. Radojcic as to the firing tables but let's recall Colonel Radojcic is the commander of the brigade. Let's recall his testimony that he had a professional officer, in fact, it was the only professional officer apart from him in that brigade, who happened to be the artillery commander, who therefore would be in charge of using the modified aerial bomb launching system with other artillery in the course of actions and would know how to use the firing tables, would know how to use the equipment. And let's recall Colonel Radojcic who stated that he fired -- that his units fired three modified aerial bombs and all three were on target. So to use Colonel Radojcic as some sort of example of these weapons being imprecise, no, they can't do that. That's not what Colonel Radojcic said. That's not what their evidence says. So you have to look at that when reaching your ultimate conclusions. Similarly, Your Honours, as the Prosecution has tried to do this entire case, they're scared of and they run away from the firing tables from the modified aerial bomb launchers, to the point now where even Mr. Tieger claims they're not in evidence. They are in evidence, Your Honours. Multiple witnesses talked about them. Defence experts referenced them and provided an excerpt. Later we got the official documents and Your Honours do have all that. And so to say they're not in evidence, really? The Prosecution's case is based upon the belief that they didn't exist but they do exist.

And I'd like to read that to you because they only mention that there was a dinner, and then 1175 talks about the decision by Mladic and other members of the JCE to separate and murder the Muslim men and boys must have been discussed and decided upon sometime between the evening of 11 July when Mladic became aware of the large --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Became aware of a number of Muslim men in Potocari who would soon come under the SF's control and the third Hotel Fontana meeting at 10.00 hours on 12 July, where he announced that the SF would be screening or inspecting the Muslim men at Potocari. Who has dinner on the morning of the 12th? No, Your Honours, they're making up the dinner. Let's continue reading what it says in 1175 --

utterances.text: I will. I'm conscious of the time that I have. In deciding to kill the able-bodied men in Potocari, Mladic would have consulted with Krstic and his senior intelligence and security officers present in Bratunac, Popovic, Kosoric, and Jankovic. And then they have footnote 5077 of their final brief for which the sole supporting evidence is General Milovanovic and several citations from the transcript. I repeat again: None of those citations say what the Prosecution claims, which is the heart of the Prosecution's case. They don't have evidence supporting it. Let's go through those citations. The first one is transcript page 16937. What did General Milovanovic say? He said at that point Mladic had regular daily meetings when he was at the Main Staff. Does that evidence a crime? No. Is Mladic at the Main Staff between the 11th and 12th of July? No. That reference has nothing to do with what the Prosecution has cited it for. The next reference, transcript page 16946 to 7. In that section Milovanovic explains that in his or Mladic's absence, the most senior chief of sector who would be in charge of the meeting would chair the meeting. Again, nothing to do with Hotel Fontana. Nothing to do with this alleged dinner that they're now making up out of thin air. Out of the thin air. Look at their brief. They have no evidence of any illegal activities discussed or agreed to by my client General Lukic -- General Mladic, I'm sorry, as to the alleged JCE to eliminate in Srebrenica. Nothing at all, Your Honours. Is that how one reaches the top of the pyramid and removes all reasonable doubt? No, Your Honours. Their case it fraught with reasonable doubt. As to the fuel order, what the Prosecution ignores is what we have detailed at paragraphs 3293 through 32 -- pardon me, 3302 of our final brief which is not only that the document P1500 comes from the operations department but, rather, that there's other information, namely from other witnesses talking about how other people could sign the general's name to things and that the initials SR did not always mean that the individual was aware of the document or that they had actually signed it. I refer you to Witness Stevanovic at transcript page 35250. He was the communications officer at the Main Staff, he would know. He stressed that people could have used the accused's signature to get an order executed even if the accused was unaware of it. That's at transcript page 35266.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm just -- I know that you're not assisted by someone who looks at timing perhaps or perhaps you are. Could you tell us where we are in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Seven to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Seven to ten minutes. Then could you just give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Stevanovic affirmed that it was possible for people to send orders under accused's name even if they did not believe this aligned with the accused's wishes. That's at transcript page 35266 of Stevanovic. Now, we have other documents in evidence that show where Mladic is during this time-period and it's not at the Main Staff. We have P364, a Prosecution document, that indicates that Mr. Mladic met with a US delegation in Dobanovci. Again, he is in Belgrade. On 13 September 1995, that's the day before the order in question at 1800 hours. Thus, we also have a document issued under General Mladic as SR signature emanating from a different number, not the operations unit, which announces the cease-fire agreement that has been reached with the Americans. So again what is General Mladic doing? Is he dealing with fuel orders? Is he dealing with Momir Nikolic's asanacija campaign? No. He is trying to negotiate peace. And let's recall Momir Nikolic's own testimony that he gave the name "asanacija" to his operation and he never once said it was from General Mladic's orders. He said from the Main Staff. It was -- if it was General Mladic, why would be he so vague? Your Honours, reasonable doubt exists as to all facets of the Prosecution's case. And rather than relying on hyperbole, I again urge you to look at our very detailed final brief which lists all of our arguments, is supported by citations to evidence, and demonstrates that for all aspects of the case, General Mladic cannot be held criminally responsible because this Prosecution has not brought you to the top of the pyramid. They've not eliminated reasonable doubt as was their burden and now they're trying to run away from that. Your Honours, I thank you for the time, and I see that I've gone over. I thank you for that indulgence. And again, I have nothing at this time to state on behalf of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. This, then, is the end of a trial which lasted for a couple of years. Before we adjourn, sine die, I wanted to -- and that's clear to you all, I think - I wanted to tell that you where a trial which is mainly oriented to the adversarial tradition, that the role of the parties is very important, and the Chamber expresses its appreciation for the parties for assisting the Chamber in performing the task which is still before us; that is, to deliver a Judgement in this case. But apart from thanking the parties, I would also like to thank the Registry and the various departments of the Registry, including Victims and Witness Section, the technicians who are assisting us, the security, all those in the Registry which have assisted us, also interpreters, translators, court reporters, all others who have made it possible to conduct this trial. The Chamber would express its appreciation for that support. We will adjourn, sine die. We stand adjourned.
